column4: uuid7.h defines two unsigned integer constants: UUID7_SIZE_BYTES, the size of an identifier, 16 bytes; and UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS, how far in milliseconds the timestamps may run ahead of the wall clock, 10000 unless the library is built with -DUUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS=<ms>. The bound is fixed into the library when it is built: defining the macro in a consumer changes only that consumer's view of the constant.
column5: Callers size their buffers and their back-off from the header, not from numbers copied out of a document.

column4: typedef int (*uuid7_rng_function_t)(void* buf, size_t n): the callback fills exactly n bytes of buf and returns 0, or returns non-zero on failure. The library calls it with n = 8 once per uuid7_gen() call, from any thread, possibly from several at once. It runs on the caller's stack inside uuid7_gen(): its frame comes on top of the budget of UUID7-SRS-053.
column5: A caller-supplied source must know what it is asked for and when.
column6: Inspection of the declaration and of its use in uuid7_gen(); the scripted-source tests call through it.

column5: The one call every consumer makes.
column6: The integration suite produces every return value: 0, -1, -2 and -3, each with the buffer checked.

A refused import leaves the source installed and the state unchanged.

column6: The integration suite produces every return value and checks that the source is installed before the import is validated.

column6: The integration suite produces every return value; the restart scenario imports through it.

column6: The integration suite installs a scripted source and restores the built-in one.

column5: Consumers link either way and keep working across minor releases.
column6: The abi-exports stage of the pipeline; the package smoke test links the installed library.

column4: Every identifier uuid7_gen() returns shall be a 16-byte binary UUID laid out as RFC 9562 section 5.7 version 7: unix_ts_ms as a 48-bit big-endian integer in bytes 0 to 5, the version 7 in the high nibble of byte 6, 12 bits of rand_a, the variant 0b10 in the two high bits of byte 8 and 62 bits of rand_b. Identifiers shall be exchanged only in this binary form; the text form (8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal) is the caller's.
column5: Consumers store, compare and transmit identifiers as 16 raw bytes and hand them to any RFC 9562 reader; one binary form keeps the interface free of formatting choices.
column6: For every identifier the integration and scenario suites generate: (byte 6 & 0xF0) == 0x70 and (byte 8 & 0xC0) == 0x80; under the test clock at 0x010203040506 ms bytes 0 to 5 decode to it; review of app/uuid7.h: no text conversion in the interface.

column4: Byte 6 of every generated identifier shall carry the version 7 (0b0111) in its high nibble.
column5: RFC 9562 version field; readers recognise the layout by it.
column6: (byte6 & 0xF0) == 0x70 for every identifier the suites generate.

column4: Byte 8 of every generated identifier shall carry the variant 0b10 in its two most significant bits.
column5: RFC 9562 variant field.
column6: (byte8 & 0xC0) == 0x80 for every identifier the suites generate.

column4: The 12-bit rand_a field (low nibble of byte 6, then byte 7) shall carry the reserved sequence value, big-endian.
column5: RFC 9562 6.2 method 1 (fixed bit-length dedicated counter) makes identifiers of one millisecond sortable.
column6: Identifiers generated in one millisecond decode to sequences 0, 1, 2, ... in generation order.

column4: The 62 bits of rand_b of every identifier shall be taken unchanged from the entropy source active for that call.
column5: Consumers expose identifiers (kyr_core's session and token identifiers) and rely on them being hard to guess from the ones issued before (SSAR asset A3); the timestamp and the counter in rand_a are guessable, so the unpredictability rests on rand_b alone. Identifiers are not secrets (SSAR R5).
column6: With a scripted source the scripted bytes appear as specified: byte 8 keeps the low six bits of the first byte, bytes 9 to 15 are the next seven bytes.

column3: Timestamp is the time of issue
column4: The timestamp of an identifier shall be the Unix time in milliseconds (CLOCK_REALTIME) at its generation, except that it may run up to UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS ahead of the clock to keep the order of UUID7-SRS-007 when the clock stalls or steps back or when more than 4096 identifiers are issued in one millisecond.
column5: Consumers read the creation time back from the identifier and sort records by it; the allowance is the price of a strict order that never waits.
column6: With the real clock and no burst the decoded timestamp lies between two CLOCK_REALTIME reads taken around the call; under the test clock a wall-clock millisecond later than the last identifier's is used as it is.

column4: Within one process, every identifier uuid7_gen() returns shall compare with memcmp() greater than every identifier returned before its call began, whatever the wall clock does; when no greater identifier can be represented (the 48-bit timestamp is exhausted) uuid7_gen() shall refuse with -3 instead of issuing one.
column5: The platform keys LMDB records by these identifiers: new records must append in byte order, and no identifier may be issued twice (SSAR asset A2).
column6: The decoded (timestamp, rand_a) pairs strictly increase and memcmp() order equals generation order in every single-thread and per-thread sequence of the suites, across sequence rollovers, a stalled clock and a clock stepped back; a reservation at the 48-bit limit returns -3 and the next call after it is unaffected.

column4: When the wall clock is later than the last reserved millisecond, the generator shall reserve the wall-clock millisecond with sequence 0.
column5: RFC 9562 6.2: the counter is reset when the timestamp advances; the timestamp tracks real time.
column6: After the test clock steps from 1000 to 1001 ms, the next identifier decodes to (1001, 0).

column4: When the wall clock equals or precedes the last reserved millisecond, the generator shall reserve the last reserved millisecond with the next sequence value.
column5: RFC 9562 6.2 monotonic error checking: a clock that stalls or steps back must not reorder identifiers.
column6: With a test clock alternating 1000 and 999 ms, 2000 identifiers decode to strictly increasing pairs.

column4: When the sequence of the last reserved millisecond is 4095, the generator shall reserve the next logical millisecond with sequence 0 instead of waiting for the wall clock.
column5: RFC 9562 6.2 counter rollover; waiting would make generation block.
column6: With a frozen clock at 1000 ms the 4097th identifier decodes to (1001, 0) and the 8193rd to (1002, 0).

column4: uuid7_gen() shall refuse with -3, leaving the reservation state unchanged, any reservation whose millisecond would exceed the wall clock by more than UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS; the bound is not applied while the clock read fails.
column5: Borrowed milliseconds must stay bounded so a burst or an abusive caller cannot date identifiers arbitrarily far in the future.
column6: With the state parked at now + UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS and sequence 4094, one more identifier is issued, then -3 twice, then success once the clock advances 1 ms.

column4: uuid7_gen() shall refuse with -3, leaving the state unchanged, any reservation whose millisecond does not fit in 48 bits.
column5: A truncated timestamp would wrap and sort before every earlier identifier.
column6: With the clock at 2^48 - 1 ms and the state at (2^48 - 1, 4094), one identifier is issued and the next two calls return -3.

column4: Two identifiers generated one after the other by one process shall compare with memcmp() in generation order.
column5: Consumers sort and key by the raw 16 bytes (RFC 9562 6.11, 6.13).
column6: memcmp(previous, next) < 0 for consecutive identifiers across sequence rollovers and clock steps, and in the installed-package smoke test.

column4: uuid7_init() with a non-NULL previous identifier shall, after installing the RNG, raise the reservation state to at least that identifier's (timestamp, sequence) pair.
column5: A restarted process must keep issuing identifiers after the ones it already stored, even when the wall clock is behind.
column6: After importing (2000, 10) with the clock at 1000 ms, the next identifier decodes to (2000, 11).

column4: uuid7_raise_floor() shall raise the reservation state as uuid7_init() does and shall leave the active RNG unchanged.
column5: The newest stored key is often known only after the database opens, long after the RNG was chosen.
column6: After importing (5000, 7) with the clock at 1000 ms, the next identifier decodes to (5000, 8) and its tail still comes from the RNG installed before.

column4: After uuid7_init() or uuid7_raise_floor() imports an identifier the caller persisted, every identifier the process then returns shall sort after the imported one and after every identifier the process returned before; an import older than the process's newest identifier shall change nothing.
column5: A restarted server, a restored snapshot or a clock set back must not issue keys that sort before the ones already stored: the consumer imports its newest stored key at start (kyr_core raises the floor from its newest key after opening its database).
column6: Identifiers generated after importing an identifier dated after the clock sort after it, through either function; importing (2000, 10) then (1000, 50) leaves the next identifier at (2000, 11); the restart scenario passes.

column4: uuid7_init() and uuid7_raise_floor() shall refuse an identifier to import that is not version 7 (-2), not of variant 0b10 (-3) or dated more than UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS after the wall clock (-4), and a refused import shall change nothing.
column5: A corrupt, foreign or future-dated stored key (a poisoned import or a runaway clock) must be a loud error at start, never a generator that dates every later identifier in the future.
column6: Each kind of invalid identifier returns its code from both functions, and the next identifier is the one the generator would have issued without the call.

column4: An imported identifier dated more than UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS after the wall clock shall be refused with -4 by uuid7_init() and uuid7_raise_floor(), leaving the state unchanged.
column5: A poisoned stored key or a runaway clock must be a loud error at start, never a generator dating everything in the future.
column6: An import at now + UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS + 1 and one at 2^48 - 1 return -4; the next identifier decodes to (now, 0).

column4: Without a caller-supplied source, rand_b shall come from the operating system's cryptographically secure generator: getrandom(2) on Linux and /dev/urandom where getrandom(2) is absent or fails.
column5: A consumer that configures nothing must still get unguessable identifiers (UUID7-SRS-005) on every platform the library builds for.
column6: Inspection of the built-in source: getrandom(2) retried on EINTR, the remainder read from /dev/urandom, a failure reported; /dev/urandom only where __linux__ is not defined.

column4: A caller shall be able to install its own entropy source at any time, through uuid7_set_rng_func() or uuid7_init(), and to restore the built-in one with NULL; the source installed last shall serve every later identifier, also when it was installed while the first identifier was being generated.
column5: Consumers with their own generator, and tests that need known tails, replace the source without rebuilding the library.
column6: A scripted source supplies the tails after either call; after NULL the built-in source serves (forced to fail, uuid7_gen() returns -2); analysis: the built-in source installed on first use never replaces a source installed concurrently; inspection of the callback contract.

column4: A caller that calls only uuid7_gen() shall get valid identifiers: initialisation is optional, and before any call the generator holds no identifier, uses the built-in entropy source on first use and counts no clock failure.
column5: Most consumers (tools, tests, small programs) have nothing to configure; a missing initialisation must not be an error.
column6: After a state reset uuid7_gen() returns 0 and a valid identifier; inspection of the initial values of the state.

column4: The lazy installation of the built-in RNG shall never replace a callback installed concurrently by uuid7_set_rng_func() or uuid7_init().
column5: A racing first generation must not undo an explicit configuration.
column6: Analysis of _ensure_rng_func(): the built-in RNG is stored by compare-and-swap from NULL only.

column4: uuid7_gen() shall obtain the random tail before it reserves a (timestamp, sequence) pair, so a failed RNG call consumes no sequence value.
column5: A sequence value consumed by a failed call would leave a gap and waste the 4096-entry space.
column6: After two failed calls in one millisecond, the next successful call decodes to the sequence right after the last successful one.

column4: When the entropy source fails, uuid7_gen() shall return -2, write nothing to the caller's buffer and leave the generator's order as it was, so that the next successful call takes the next sequence value; no identifier shall carry partial or zeroed entropy.
column5: A consumer must be able to retry or fail its request without a weak identifier slipping into its keys or tokens.
column6: With a failing caller-supplied source and with the built-in source forced to fail: -2, the buffer keeps its bytes, and the next success takes the next sequence value; inspection: the built-in source zeroes what it could not fill before it reports the failure.

column4: When the built-in RNG fails, it shall zero every byte it could not fill before returning the failure.
column5: Uninitialised or partial bytes must not look like entropy, even inside the library.
column6: Inspection of _default_rng(): every failure return is preceded by memset() of the unfilled suffix.

column4: When the wall clock cannot be read, uuid7_gen() shall keep issuing identifiers in the order of UUID7-SRS-007, their timestamps no longer advancing, and count the failure; uuid7_clock_failure_count() shall return the number of failures since the process started: 0 on a healthy clock, never decreasing.
column5: Losing the clock must not stop a server or break its keys; the frozen timestamps are misleading, so the consumer needs a counter to alert on.
column6: Inspection of the clock-failure path: the failed read counted and taken as 0, the ahead bound skipped, the reservation continued from the state; uuid7_clock_failure_count() returns 0 throughout the suites on a healthy clock.

column4: uuid7_clock_failure_count() shall return the number of clock_gettime() failures since process start, 0 on a healthy clock.
column5: Operators alert on a non-zero value.
column6: After a generation with the real clock the count is 0.

column4: Every function of the interface shall be callable concurrently from any number of threads; no two calls in one process shall return the same identifier, each identifier's rand_b shall come from one entropy source, and the identifiers of each thread shall keep the order of UUID7-SRS-007, entropy-source changes and floor imports racing included.
column5: The platform's servers generate identifiers on many threads with no lock of their own and may change the entropy source while running.
column6: 16 threads x 100000 identifiers: every thread's sequence strictly increases and all identifiers are distinct; entropy-source swaps and floor imports racing generation break neither; the concurrent scenario passes.

column4: uuid7_set_rng_func(), uuid7_init() and uuid7_raise_floor() shall be safe to call concurrently with uuid7_gen(); each generation shall use one callback for its whole tail.
column5: Configuration may change while workers run.
column6: With one thread changing the RNG and re-importing a floor, 4 x 100000 identifiers are distinct and per-thread ordered; the callback pointer is loaded once per call.

column4: uuid7_gen() shall never block, sleep, take a lock or wait for the wall clock to advance; under contention some call shall always complete.
column5: Callers generate identifiers on request paths and inside their own critical sections: a generator that waits stalls them, one that locks can deadlock with them.
column6: Analysis of uuid7_gen(): no lock, no sleep, no wait; the loop repeats only after a failed compare-and-swap, which means another call succeeded or the weak form failed spuriously; the same-millisecond scenario moves to the next logical millisecond without the clock advancing.

column4: uuid7_gen(NULL) shall return -1.
column5: A missing buffer is a caller error reported, not a crash.
column6: uuid7_gen(NULL) returns -1.

column4: uuid7_raise_floor(NULL) shall return -1.
column5: A missing floor is a caller error reported, not a crash.
column6: uuid7_raise_floor(NULL) returns -1.

column4: On the release build, in one thread, the mean cost of one uuid7_gen() call, the entropy source's own time excluded, shall not exceed 100 ns on the reference workstation.
column5: Identifier generation sits on every write path of the platform; the budget keeps the generator's own share negligible. The entropy source is the caller's choice and is measured apart.
column6: tests/stress/stress.c with its benchmark source, release profile, static linkage: mean cost per identifier <= 100 ns (tests/results/stress/stress_summary.tsv).

column4: uuid7_gen() shall issue at least 4096 identifiers per millisecond of the wall clock and absorb a burst of up to 4096 x UUID7_MAX_AHEAD_MS identifiers ahead of it; beyond that it shall refuse with -3, change nothing, and issue again once the clock has caught up.
column5: Consumers insert in bulk (imports, migrations) faster than the clock advances: they need a known capacity and a refusal they can back off from, never a stall or a silent loss of order. With the default bound the burst is 40,960,000 identifiers.
column6: Under the test clock 4096 identifiers take one logical millisecond and the next one the following millisecond; at the bound uuid7_gen() returns -3 with the state unchanged and succeeds again after the clock advances; analysis of the reservation rule gives the burst size.

column4: The library shall hold at most 24 bytes of static data on x86-64 and no thread-local storage.
column5: A foundation library linked into every product: a fixed footprint needs no initialisation, no teardown and no allocation.
column6: nm and size of the release object: the static data objects sum to at most 24 bytes; no thread-local section.

column4: The library shall not allocate memory and shall hold no file descriptor between calls: a descriptor it opens to read entropy shall be opened close-on-exec and closed before the call returns.
column5: The caller owns every buffer, and a server that forks or executes children must not leak descriptors it does not know of.
column6: nm -D --undefined-only on the release libuuid7.so lists none of malloc, calloc, realloc, free, aligned_alloc, posix_memalign; inspection of the entropy fallback: O_CLOEXEC, and close() on every path.

column4: The library shall depend at run time on the C library only and know nothing of the platform: it shall include only C library and POSIX headers and perform no I/O but reading the entropy source.
column5: A foundation library (tier 1) pulls nothing else into its consumers and can be reused outside the platform.
column6: readelf -d on the release libuuid7.so lists exactly one NEEDED entry, libc.so.6; the #include lines of app/uuid7.c name C library and POSIX headers only.

column4: One call of any interface function shall use at most 256 bytes of the caller's stack on x86-64 (release build, built-in entropy source).
column5: Consumers call the generator from deep call chains and on small thread stacks.
column6: gcc -fstack-usage on the release build: every frame static, and the deepest chain from an interface function through the functions it calls or references, the built-in entropy source included, is at most 256 bytes.

column4: The release object of the library shall hold at most 4096 bytes of code (.text).
column5: A foundation library linked into every product of the platform must stay small.
column6: size of the release object app__uuid7.c.o: text <= 4096 bytes.

column4: The library and its header shall be ISO C11 and compile without any warning under every profile of the pinned kyr-build catalog.
column5: Consumers build with -Werror and include uuid7.h in their own translation units; the catalog's warning set is the static analysis of the code.
column6: No line with warning: in the build logs of the six profiles (build/pipeline/build_*.log).

column6: Inspection of _default_rng(): open(..., O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC) and close() on success and on both failure paths.

column5: The library stays portable to other POSIX systems.
column6: Inspection of the #ifdef __linux__ branches of _default_rng().

column4: The library shall build and work on any platform with an ISO C11 compiler, 64-bit atomic compare-and-swap, clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) and /dev/urandom, and shall fail to build on a platform without 8-bit bytes or a 64-bit uint64_t.
column5: The library is reused beyond its first platform (Linux x86-64, where it is qualified); a platform the layout code cannot serve must fail at build time, never produce wrong identifiers.
column6: Inspection: the static assertions of app/uuid7.c; the only Linux-specific call, getrandom(2), is guarded by __linux__ and has the /dev/urandom fallback.

column4: Every interface function shall report failure only through its return value (a negative code the ICD lists), never through errno, a signal, abort() or output, and a failed call shall change neither the generator's state nor the caller's buffer.
column5: Consumers handle every failure on their own code path; a library that logs, aborts or half-writes takes that decision from them.
column6: Inspection of every return path of app/uuid7.c; the tests produce each documented code (NULL buffer -1, NULL floor -1, entropy -2, bound and range -3, imports -2, -3 and -4) and check that nothing was written or changed.
